issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s constitutional writ challenging a finding of deemed vacancy is not premature when the governing statutory scheme provides no adequate or effective remedy for challenging that finding.
material_facts: In each proceeding, a tenant of non-residential premises was found to have caused a deemed vacancy by admitting a person related by marriage into the business partnership.
The tenants challenged the deemed-vacancy findings, but the High Court dismissed their writ petitions as premature on the basis that later statutory remedies were available.
The statutory revision lay against a final allotment or release order, not against notification of vacancy, and its grounds were narrower than those available in an appeal.

A tenant’s opportunity to contest whether the deemed-vacancy provision applied was not assured before a release order, and the same vacancy finding could not effectively be reopened in a later revision.
issues.conclusion: The tenants’ writ petitions under Articles 226 and 227 were not premature; the High Court was required to hear them on their merits.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 12(2) and 12(4) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, a qualifying partnership change may result in a deemed vacancy. The proviso to Section 16(1) provides a hearing before an allotment order in specified deemed-vacancy cases, but does not provide the same hearing before release to the landlord. Section 18, as substituted by the 1976 amendment, provides revision against a final allotment or release order on grounds corresponding to Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and not against notification of vacancy. Section 16(5) review and the later revision do not provide an adequate substitute for contesting the vacancy finding before it is acted upon. Accordingly, a tenant may challenge that finding by a writ petition under Articles 226 or 227. The Court stated that the correctness of Trilok Singh & Co. v. District Magistrate, Lucknow was open to doubt, particularly because it overlooked Rule 8 and treated later review or appeal as adequate remedies.

predicates.tenant_writ_challenges_deemed_vacancy: A tenant files a constitutional writ challenging an authority’s finding that the premises are deemed vacant.
predicates.no_effective_statutory_review: The statutory process provides no effective means to contest the vacancy finding before it is acted upon, and later review or revision cannot adequately reopen that finding.
predicates.writ_is_not_premature: The tenant’s writ challenge may be heard without waiting for a later allotment or release order.

issues.definition: When a tenant uses a constitutional writ to challenge a deemed-vacancy finding and the statutory process offers no effective review of that finding, the writ is not premature.

issues.legal_issue: Before notifying a vacancy, the authority must comply with the prescribed procedure for public notice and must decide any objection received within the prescribed objection period.
material_facts: The statutory rules prescribed inspection of premises alleged to be vacant and required the inspection report’s conclusion to be posted for public information.
The rules allowed objections to be received before notification and required any objection received to be decided after considering evidence the objector or another concerned person might present.
The tenants sought to contest the deemed-vacancy findings and relied on the procedural opportunity provided by the rules.
issues.conclusion: The prescribed hearing opportunity must be afforded before the vacancy is notified; notifying the vacancy without first following the objection procedure violates Rule 8.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 8 of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972, requires inspection before an allotment or release order, public posting of the inspection conclusion, and a minimum period before allotment; if an objection is received in that period, it must be disposed of after considering relevant evidence. The Court observed that the corresponding original rule had the same effect. It therefore disagreed with the observation in Trilok Singh & Co. v. District Magistrate, Lucknow that a hearing before notification was unnecessary, and said the correctness of that decision was open to doubt.

predicates.vacancy_determination_proceeding: An authority is determining whether premises alleged to be vacant should be notified as vacant.
predicates.objection_pending: A concerned person has submitted an objection within the period before notification, and the authority has not yet decided it.
predicates.notification_must_wait_for_objection_dec: The authority must decide the objection before notifying the vacancy.

issues.definition: When an authority is determining whether premises are vacant and an objection remains undecided, notification must await the decision on that objection.
